a: to a woman named Rhoda
p: Sinaiticus names Hermas's owner Rhoda; the Athos manuscript and one Latin version just say 'a certain woman'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); Lake's text
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1)

why: The oldest manuscript has the name, and Lake follows it. Lake's footnote says the other reading is 'omitting the mention of her name'. A scribe is more likely to drop a strange personal name than to invent one.
b: Rhoda is also the name of the servant girl in Acts 12:13; the name was common.

a: Cumae
p: The Greek Komas can be the town of Cumae or simply 'the villages'; the Latin has 'the city of Ostia'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s), the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text, read as the town (his English: 'Cumae')
the same Greek read as a common noun (Lake's alternative)
readings.en: to the villages, out to the country

readings.w: both Latin versions (L)

why: Lake prints the word with a capital and translates 'Cumae'. His footnote: 'the editors emend to Κούμας (Cumae). It is probable that Cumae is the meaning of the text, but it is not impossible the spelling κώμας is original. The alternative is that πορευομένου εἰς κώμας means the same as the modern Italian "Villeggiatura" (summer holiday in the country).' At 5:1 the Latin has 'the region of Cumae', which supports the town.
b: Cumae, a Greek colony near Naples, was the seat of the Cumaean Sibyl, the prophetess Hermas thinks he has met (8:1). Ostia was Rome's port at the mouth of the Tiber. If the word means 'the villages', Hermas was only going out to the country, as he goes 'out to the country' in 22:2.

a: Where, or when
p: Sinaiticus's first hand and the Vulgate Latin ask 'where'; the corrector, the Athos manuscript and the Palatine Latin 'in what way'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand; the Vulgate Latin (L1); Lake's text
a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), the Palatine Latin (L2) (and the Ethiopic, as Lake reports it)

why: Lake follows the first hand of Sinaiticus. 'In what place or when' is a natural pair of questions; the two Greek words differ by one letter, so a copyist could easily write one for the other.

a: a goddess
p: Hermas says he honored Rhoda 'as a goddess'; the Athos manuscript has 'daughter', the Ethiopic 'lady'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); Lake's text
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s)
the Ethiopic (E) (Lake gives it in Latin)

why: Lake follows Sinaiticus and translates 'Did I not always look on you as a goddess?' 'Goddess' is the harder reading: a Christian scribe had reason to change it, and none to put it in.
b: The Greek thean is 'goddess'. It is an odd word for a Christian; Hermas uses it to say he never thought of her in any low way. 'Daughter' would not fit a woman who had once owned him.

a: You let it go to ruin
p: The Athos manuscript, the Latin and the Ethiopic add 'terribly'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand; the Amherst papyrus; Lake's text
readings.plain: You let it go to ruin

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); both Latin versions; the Ethiopic (E)
readings.en: you let it be terribly ruined
readings.plain: You let it go terribly to ruin

why: The shorter reading has the oldest witnesses, the first hand of Sinaiticus and the Amherst papyrus, an early copy on papyrus. Adding a word for emphasis is a common change in copying.

a: whom I love
p: Lake: 'The text is clearly corrupt, and cannot be restored with certainty.' Each version reads differently.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); Lake's text
the Vulgate Latin (L1) (Lake: = Greek ἀοράτῳ)
the Palatine Latin (L2)
readings.en: who upholds all things by power
readings.plain: who holds up all things by his power

readings.w: the Ethiopic (E) (Lake's English)
readings.en: in his pity and in his love
readings.plain: in his pity and his love

why: Lake's footnote cites only Sinaiticus for the Greek, prints it, and marks the place as corrupt. The Plain English Translation follows his text. The Latin of L1 points to a Greek word meaning 'invisible', which would fit 11:5 ('the unseen power of the Master').

a: the first ones were hard and harsh
p: Lake prints 'the first' (πρῶτα) here against the witnesses, from an inference about the manuscript A was copied from.

readings.w: Lake's text (his conjecture for the archetype of A)
readings.plain: the first ones were hard and harsh

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin (L, priora); a hand of Codex Sinaiticus
readings.plain: the earlier ones were hard and harsh

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, as Lake reports it (one hand)
readings.plain: the rest were hard and harsh

why: Lake's footnote: A reads πρότερα and the Latin priora, Sinaiticus omits the word, 'but the next line (where A also reads πρότερα) suggests that its archetype read πρῶτα.' So Lake prints πρῶτα, 'the first', from an inference about the copy behind A. The sense is the same on either reading: the opening words of the reading, against 'these last words'.

a: Cumae
p: The Latin here has 'the region of Cumae', which supports Cumae at 1:3. Goes with the variant at 1:3.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s), the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text (his English 'Cumae')
both Latin versions (L)
readings.en: the region of the people of Cumae

readings.w: the same Greek read as a common noun

why: As at 1:3, Lake prints the place name and translates 'Cumae'. His footnote here gives the Latin 'regionem Cumanorum', 'but see the note on Vis. I. 1. 3', where he allows that the word may mean only 'the villages'.

a: I had seen the year before
p: Sinaiticus says Hermas had seen her 'before'; the Athos manuscript and the Vulgate Latin 'the year before'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); Lake's text
readings.plain: I had seen the year before

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
the Ethiopic (E); the Palatine Latin (L2)

why: Lake follows A and the Vulgate Latin. 'Last year' agrees with 5:1, where the vision is 'at the same season as the year before', so either reading says the same thing.

a: then all the sins
p: Sinaiticus and the Palatine Latin read 'when', which does not fit the sentence; the others read 'then'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Palatine Latin (L2)

why: The sentence needs 'then': after Hermas makes the words known, then the sins are forgiven. The two Greek words differ in one letter.

a: their Christ
p: The only place 'Christ' stands in the Shepherd, and only in Sinaiticus's first hand. Others read 'Lord' or 'Son'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand; Lake's text
a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), the Palatine Latin (L2)
the Vulgate Latin (L1)

why: Lake prints the first hand of Sinaiticus, the oldest witness. It is also the harder reading: everywhere else the book says 'the Lord' or 'the Son of God', and a corrector who knew that would change 'Christ' to 'Lord' to match. The Vulgate Latin's 'the Son' picks up 'his Son' just before.
b: Checked by script in Lake's Greek and Latin: neither 'Jesus' nor 'Christ' stands anywhere else in the Shepherd. The book speaks of 'the Son of God' (Similitudes 5 and 9), 'the Lord' and 'the Name' (9:9; 23:4). So the reading matters for how the book names the one it worships. If 'their Christ' is original, Hermas knew and used the title, but chose for the rest of his book the language of Son and Lord. If 'their Lord' is original, the Shepherd never names Christ at all. Either way, 'deny' and 'his Son' in the same verse make plain who is meant.

a: Eldad and Modat
p: The witnesses spell the two prophets' names in several ways; Numbers 11:26 has Eldad and Medad.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); Lake's text
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s)
the Vulgate Latin (L1)
the Palatine Latin (L2)
a form Lake gives with the siglum A, which he has already used for the Greek Ἐλὰδ καὶ Μωδάδ

why: Lake follows Sinaiticus. His footnote lists five forms; the last, 'Eldad et Mudath', is a Latin form, though the siglum printed with it is A. The two men are Eldad and Medad of Numbers 11:26 (the Greek Bible spells the second Modad); the Plain English Translation keeps the book's own spelling here, 'Modat', so the reader sees what the manuscript has.

a: She stood beside me
p: Lake prints the Athos manuscript's 'stood'; the Latin and Ethiopic say 'stood behind me'; most editors emend to 'stood over'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); Lake's text
the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E)
an emendation 'accepted by most editors' (Lake)

why: Lake keeps the manuscript's word and notes the editors' change. Sinaiticus is not cited for the word in his footnote.

a: the Name
p: The Greek manuscripts read 'my name' or 'his name'; Lake prints the Vulgate Latin's 'the Name'.

readings.w: the Vulgate Latin (L1); Lake's text
a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus; and in another order Codex Sinaiticus, first hand
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Palatine Latin (L2); the Ethiopic (E)

why: Lake's text follows the shortest reading. 'The Name' standing alone is the usual early Christian way to speak of Christ's name (Acts 5:41), and in 10:1 the phrase stands again with no 'my' or 'his'. Scribes often add a pronoun to make such phrases clear, and the two Greek forms add different ones.

a: by the six young men
p: The first hand of Sinaiticus says sixty young men built the tower; all others, and Sinaiticus itself at 12:2, say six.

readings.w: a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus, the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s), the Latin and the Ethiopic; Lake's text
Codex Sinaiticus, first hand

why: Six is the number in 9:6 and 12:1-2, and Lake's footnote at 12:1 notes that 'in the next verse' Sinaiticus too reads six. The first hand of Sinaiticus has 'sixty' twice in 10:5 and again in 12:1.

a: Others they smashed and threw far from the tower
p: Sinaiticus says they 'set' the broken stones far from the tower; the others say 'threw'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.plain: Others they smashed and threw far from the tower

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
readings.plain: Others they smashed and set far from the tower

why: 'Threw' agrees with 10:9 and 14:1 ('thrown far from the tower'). Sinaiticus's 'set' repeats the verb of the sentence before ('set some into the building'), an easy slip for a copyist.

a: Then they will be more cheerful, and when they hear these things they will know the Lord in his great glory.
t: A shorter text in Sinaiticus and the Ethiopic
p: Sinaiticus and the Ethiopic lack 'they will be more cheerful, and these things' and change the next words.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin (L); Lake's text
readings.orig: καὶ ἱλαρώτεροι γένωνται καὶ ταῦτα ἀκούσαντες γινώσκωσιν τὸν κύριον ἐν πολλῇ δόξῃ
readings.en: and they may become more cheerful, and having heard these things may know the Lord in great glory
readings.plain: Then they will be more cheerful, and when they hear these things they will know the Lord in his great glory.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Ethiopic (E)
readings.orig: ἐν πολλῇ δόξῃ, ἔφη, ἀκούσονται κ.τ.λ. (without ἱλαρώτεροι γένωνται, καὶ ταῦτα)
readings.en: 'in great glory,' she said, 'they will hear ...'

why: Lake prints the text of A and the Latin and gives the other in his footnote; he does not print the whole of the Sinaiticus sentence, so its English here is only the words he quotes. Sinaiticus leaves out short passages often in these chapters (see 24:5).

a: the name of the Lord
p: Sinaiticus reads 'the name of God'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; Lake's text
Codex Sinaiticus (300s)

why: Lake follows A and the Latin here against Sinaiticus. The two words were written in short forms in manuscripts, and are often exchanged.

a: because wickedness has been found in them
p: Sinaiticus says the angels warn them because wickedness was found in them; the other witnesses say because none was found.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); Lake's text
readings.en: because wickedness was found in them
readings.plain: because wickedness has been found in them

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E)
readings.en: because no wickedness was found in them
readings.plain: because no wickedness has been found in them

why: Lake prints Sinaiticus and translates 'because wickedness has been found in them'. On that reading the young believers are being built in but still need warning; on the other, they are being built in because they are innocent. 'Not found' may be a scribe's change to make the faithful stones sound better.

a: did not stay in it
t: A longer text about the scabby stones
p: The Athos manuscript and the Vulgate Latin add 'and do not keep close to the saints; that is why they are useless'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Palatine Latin (L2); the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1)
readings.orig: αὐτῇ, μηδὲ κολλώμενοι τοῖς ἁγίοις. διὰ τοῦτο ἄχρηστοί εἰσιν
readings.en: ... in it, nor clinging to the saints; for this reason they are useless
readings.plain: did not stay in it or keep close to the saints. That is why they are no use

why: Lake follows the shorter text of Sinaiticus, the Palatine Latin and the Ethiopic. The added words look like an explanation drawn from the language of the context (compare 14:7, 'no use').

a: the wealth of this world. When suffering comes, they deny their Lord because of their wealth and their business dealings.
p: Sinaiticus lacks 'of this world. When suffering comes, ... because of their wealth', so the denial is not tied to persecution.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); Lake's text
readings.orig: πλοῦτον τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου· ὅταν γένηται θλῖψις, διὰ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτῶν
readings.en: wealth of this age; when trouble comes, because of their wealth
readings.plain: the wealth of this world. When suffering comes, they deny their Lord because of their wealth and their business dealings.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
readings.en: their wealth, and because of their business dealings they deny their Lord
readings.plain: their wealth, and because of their business dealings they deny their Lord.

why: Lake's footnote marks the words as missing in Sinaiticus only. The gap runs from one 'wealth' (πλοῦτον) to the next, the kind of skip a copyist's eye makes between two like words. Without them Sinaiticus says nothing of persecution here.

a: For you yourself are being used as one of these very stones.
t: The obscure sentence missing in Sinaiticus
p: Sinaiticus lacks the whole sentence that Lake calls obscure.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); Lake's text
readings.orig: καὶ γὰρ σὺ αὐτὸς χρᾶσαι ἐκ τῶν αὐτῶν λίθων
readings.en: for you yourself are used from the same stones
readings.plain: For you yourself are being used as one of these very stones.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)

why: Lake prints the sentence and notes that Sinaiticus omits it. In his English footnote the Greek 'is obscure and the early translations all paraphrase it so freely that they cannot be used to suggest any emendation' (see the note). Without it, 14:7 ends with 'Be useful to God, all of you.'

a: because of the evil works they did
p: Lake: Sinaiticus's text 'can scarcely be quite correct', but the other reading 'is clearly an emendation'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Palatine Latin (L2); Lake's text
readings.orig: διὰ τὰ ἔργα ἃ εἰργάσαντο πονηρά
readings.en: because of the evil works which they did
readings.plain: because of the evil works they did

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E)
readings.orig: ἐὰν ἀναβῇ ἐπὶ τὴν καρδίαν αὐτῶν (in place of διά)
readings.en: if the works they did come up into their heart
readings.plain: if the evil works they did come into their hearts

why: Lake keeps the reading of Sinaiticus and the Palatine Latin, though it hardly makes sense, because the other is a scribe's repair. His English footnote: 'Apparently the meaning is "Then, i.e. if they repent", but the text is obscure, and probably some words have been lost.' The Plain English Translation renders Lake's words as they stand.

a: believing that if he keeps away from every evil desire he will inherit eternal life
p: Sinaiticus has a simpler sentence: he will keep away from every evil work and evil desire, and will inherit eternal life.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.orig: πιστεύων ὅτι, ἐὰν ἀφέξηται πάσης ἐπιθυμίας πονηρᾶς, κληρονομήσει ζωὴν αἰώνιον
readings.en: believing that, if he abstains from every evil desire, he will inherit eternal life
readings.plain: believing that if he keeps away from every evil desire he will inherit eternal life

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
readings.orig: καὶ (for πιστεύων ὅτι ἐὰν ἀφέξηται); καὶ κληρονομήσει
readings.en: and from every evil desire, and he will inherit eternal life
readings.plain: and from every evil desire, and he will inherit eternal life

why: Lake follows the fuller text of A, the Latin and the Ethiopic. The sense is close: on both readings self-control leads to eternal life.

a: And I command you first, Hermas, to speak all these words I am about to tell you into the ears of the saints
p: Sinaiticus and the Vulgate Latin lack 'I command you first'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); Lake's text
readings.en: and I command you first, Hermas
readings.plain: And I command you first, Hermas, to speak all these words I am about to tell you into the ears of the saints

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Vulgate Latin (L1)
readings.en: Hermas, ... to speak all these words
readings.plain: Hermas, speak all these words I am about to tell you into the ears of the saints

why: Lake prints the words and gives the omission in his footnote. 'First' (πρῶτον) also ends the clause before ('you must understand them first'), so a copyist's eye could jump from one to the other. The sense is the same: Hermas is to speak the words to the saints.

a: to the Lord
t: The Lord, our Lord, your Lord
p: The Greek manuscripts add 'our' or 'your'; Lake prints the plain 'the Lord' of the Vulgate Latin and the Ethiopic.

readings.w: the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Palatine Latin (L2)

why: The two Greek manuscripts disagree, adding different words that sounded alike in later Greek. Lake prints the reading without either, which explains both.

a: and she was more cheerful than before
t: Cheerful than before, or in face
p: Sinaiticus reads 'more cheerful in face'.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.orig: ἱλαρωτέρα δὲ ἦν ἢ τὸ πρότερον
readings.en: she was more cheerful than before
readings.plain: and she was more cheerful than before

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
readings.en: she was more cheerful in face
readings.plain: and she was more cheerful in face

why: Lake follows the majority. 20:1 repeats the description with 'more cheerful than before' (hilarōteran para to proteron), which supports it.

a: about the forms you are asking about
t: The forms, or the three forms
p: A corrector of Sinaiticus and the Athos manuscript add 'three'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand; the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.plain: about the forms you are asking about

readings.w: a corrector of Codex Sinaiticus; the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s)
readings.plain: about the three forms you are asking about

why: The shorter text is the older; 'three' is easily added from 18:2 and 18:9.

a: Do not ask anything more about revelation.
p: Sinaiticus and the Palatine Latin lack 'about revelation': 'Do not ask anything more.'

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.plain: Do not ask anything more about revelation.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Palatine Latin (L2)

why: Lake follows A, the Vulgate Latin and the Ethiopic. Both readings close the subject; the longer one limits the ban to more revelation, which fits the next words ('if anything is needed, it will be revealed to you'). The words bear on what the book says about its own revelation being complete (compare 11:2).

a: It was a figure of the suffering that is coming.
t: The figure of the coming suffering
p: Sinaiticus lacks the words that say what Vision 4 means.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.orig: εἰς τύπον τῆς θλίψεως τῆς ἐπερχομένης
readings.en: for a figure of the suffering that is coming
readings.plain: It was a figure of the suffering that is coming.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s) (and in part the Palatine Latin)

why: Lake prints the words. They agree with 23:5 and 24:6 ('a figure of the great suffering'), so the meaning of the vision is the same with or without them.

a: the great and glorious Name
t: Through the Name, or through the holy angel?
p: Sinaiticus reads 'through the holy angel and glorious name', making the angel a means of salvation.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.orig: διὰ τοῦ μεγάλου καὶ ἐνδόξου ὀνόματος
readings.en: through the great and glorious name

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)
readings.en: through the holy angel and glorious name
readings.plain: the holy angel and the glorious Name

why: Lake follows the majority. 'The great and glorious name' stands in 22:3 too. Sinaiticus's reading may come from the angel Thegri named in the next sentence.

a: who live in the midst of them, the blood and the fire
p: Sinaiticus and the Latin say 'among them' (the blood and the fire); the Athos manuscript and the Ethiopic 'in it' (the world).

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Latin; Lake's text
readings.plain: who live in the midst of them, the blood and the fire

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Ethiopic (E)

why: Lake prints the harder reading and explains in his English footnote: 'The "them" means "fire and blood"; but the construction of the sentence is awkward.' 'In it' (this world) is the easier text a scribe would make.

a: , for those whom God has chosen for eternal life will be spotless and pure
p: Sinaiticus lacks the clause about the chosen being spotless and pure.

readings.w: the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Latin; the Ethiopic (E); Lake's text
readings.orig: ὅτι ἄσπιλοι καὶ καθαροὶ ἔσονται οἱ ἐκλελεγμένοι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον
readings.en: because spotless and pure will be those chosen by God for eternal life
readings.plain: , for those whom God has chosen for eternal life will be spotless and pure

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s)

why: Lake prints the clause. Lake records Sinaiticus leaving out short passages all through these chapters (among them 11:1, 12:3, 14:1, 14:5, 14:7, 16:11, 18:8, 20:2, 21:4 and 24:7; the larger ones have their own entries), so its gaps are not taken as the original text.

a: for a cloud came
p: Sinaiticus and the Palatine Latin say 'a cloud'; the Athos manuscript, the Vulgate Latin and the Ethiopic 'a noise'.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (300s); the Palatine Latin (L2); Lake's text
the Athos manuscript (A, 1400s); the Vulgate Latin (L1); the Ethiopic (E)

why: Lake follows the cloud. It explains why Hermas could not see where she went; a noise explains why he turned around in fear, thinking the beast was coming. Both fit, and the witnesses are evenly split.
